# Do Safety Policies Make Falsifiable Predictions? A Commitment-Tracking Harness

**Problem:** Safety commitments are only meaningful if you can later check whether they were honored, yet there is no public ledger that converts policy language into trackable, testable predictions with deadlines.

**Direction:** Parse public safety policies and extract every commitment that contains a temporal or conditional trigger ('before deployment we will...', 'by Q2 we will publish...'). Use an LLM to classify each into testable/untestable and, for testable ones, into 'verifiable from public evidence' vs 'requires private access'. Cross-reference against subsequently published model/system cards to mark which testable-public commitments were actually evidenced. Output a small structured dataset plus a blog post on the falsifiability rate.

**Why it matters:** Turns aspirational governance text into an accountability instrument that anyone can maintain, directly attacking the 'vague commitments' and 'verification by third parties' open problems without needing model access or lab cooperation.

**Relevant context:** METR common-elements reports; FLI AI Safety Index emphasis on 'implemented assessments, not stated commitments'; California SB 53 transparency obligations.

# Replicating the AI Safety Index Across an Overlooked Dimension: Whistleblowing & Internal Dissent

**Problem:** FLI's AI Safety Index scores labs across six domains but does not isolate the institutional mechanisms (whistleblower protections, non-disparagement clauses, internal escalation paths) that let safety concerns surface — a dimension that recent lab controversies suggest is decisive.

**Direction:** Apply the Index's public-evidence methodology to a new 'internal dissent & whistleblowing' dimension. Build ~8 indicators (existence of whistleblower policy, public non-disparagement commitments, board safety oversight, anonymous reporting channels) and score each frontier lab from public sources, validating coding with a second annotator. Produce a mini-index and compare its ranking to the official Index.

**Why it matters:** Whether employees can safely raise alarms is a medium-horizon governance lever frontier labs deprioritize; measuring it from public evidence is exactly the kind of diffuse, fuzzy-reward evaluation that needs no lab resources and complements existing indices.

**Relevant context:** FLI AI Safety Index Summer/Winter 2025 (33 indicators, 6 domains, public-evidence methodology); Generation Strategy Hint FR67 (apply Index methodology to additional dimensions).

# Capability-Threshold Cartography: Are Lab 'Red Lines' Mutually Consistent?

**Problem:** Each frontier safety policy defines its own dangerous-capability thresholds (CBRN uplift, cyber-offense, autonomous replication), but no one has mapped whether these thresholds are commensurable — a model could cross OpenAI's line while staying under Anthropic's, undermining any shared regulatory floor.

**Direction:** Extract every capability threshold and its trigger criteria from public policies into a normalized schema (capability domain, metric, threshold value, response action). Use an LLM to align analogous thresholds across labs and flag where definitions diverge or are non-operational. Produce a comparison matrix and quantify the 'consistency gap', highlighting domains with no shared definition.

**Why it matters:** International coordination and enforceable standards require commensurable thresholds; surfacing the incommensurability is a concrete contribution to the 'international consensus on evaluation methodologies' open problem, done entirely from public text.

**Relevant context:** METR common-elements analysis of capability thresholds; arXiv:2512.01166 framework evaluation; International Network of AI Safety Institutes joint testing exercises.

# An Open Reproduction of 'Common Elements' Scoring as a Living Diff Tool

**Problem:** METR's Common Elements reports are periodic PDF snapshots; the field lacks a lightweight, reproducible pipeline that detects how a single lab's safety policy text changes between versions and whether changes strengthen or weaken commitments.

**Direction:** Collect archived versions of one or two labs' safety policies (via Wayback Machine / git of public repos). Build a diff + LLM-classification pipeline that labels each textual change as strengthening, weakening, clarifying, or cosmetic, with a rubric. Validate on a hand-labeled subset and report the trajectory of commitment strength over time.

**Why it matters:** Continuous monitoring of policy erosion is a strategically valuable, low-cost governance infrastructure that no lab will build about itself; it directly supports third-party accountability and is fully reproducible from public archives.

**Relevant context:** METR Common Elements Mar 2025 and Dec 2025 updates; ailabwatch.org commitments tracker; California SB 53 framework-disclosure requirement.

# Measuring the Model-Card Transparency Gap with a Public Scoring Pipeline

**Problem:** AI documentation is fragmented and inconsistent (one study found 947 unique section names; 'usage' alone appeared under 97 labels), but most labs and policymakers lack a simple, reproducible score for how much safety-critical information a given model card actually discloses.

**Direction:** Reimplement a stripped-down version of the AI Transparency Atlas weighted rubric (safety evaluation, critical risk, intended use, limitations) and run it over 20-40 publicly available model/system cards from HuggingFace and frontier labs. Use an LLM to detect presence/quality of each section against the rubric and compute compliance scores, reporting where open vs closed providers diverge.

**Why it matters:** Cheap, auditable transparency scoring lets regulators operationalize EU AI Act Annex IV and California SB 53 disclosure expectations; it needs only public cards and no model access, maximizing counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** AI Transparency Atlas arXiv:2512.12443 (8 sections/23 subsections, EU AI Act Annex IV baseline); Stanford FMTI; California SB 53 / EU GPAI Code of Practice transparency section.

# Do Disclosed Safety Evaluations Actually Report Negative Results?

**Problem:** Model cards list safety evaluations but it is unknown how often they report failures, refusals to deploy, or capabilities that crossed thresholds — publication bias in safety reporting would make cards a misleading basis for governance.

**Direction:** Assemble a corpus of frontier model/system cards. For each reported safety eval, use an LLM to classify the outcome framing (pass-only, mixed, explicit failure/limitation disclosed) and whether mitigations are described. Quantify the rate of negative-result disclosure across labs and over time, with a hand-labeled validation set, and discuss what a healthy disclosure norm would look like.

**Why it matters:** If safety cards are systematically positive-framed, regulators relying on them for compliance are being misled; documenting this from public sources is a diffuse, fuzzy-reward evaluation with strong counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** FLI Index focus on 'implemented assessments'; AI Transparency Atlas; 'Frontier AI Auditing' GovAI paper on verifying developer claims.

**Problem:** The OECD's common reporting framework argues near-misses should be reported because they share characteristics with incidents, but the existing AI Incident Database does not cleanly distinguish near-misses from realized harms, limiting their use for proactive governance.

**Direction:** Pull a sample of public AIID / OECD AIM entries and use an LLM with a clear rubric to classify each as realized-harm vs near-miss vs hazard, plus the lifecycle stage and harm type. Measure how prevalent near-miss reporting actually is, where it is missing, and propose minimal schema additions. Validate coding against human labels and report agreement.

**Why it matters:** Aviation-style incident response (an explicit open problem) depends on capturing near-misses; quantifying the current gap from a public open-source database is foundational governance infrastructure requiring no lab access.

**Relevant context:** OECD common reporting framework (29 criteria, near-miss scope); AIID open-source database; CSET 'AI Incidents: Key Components' Jan 2025; arXiv:2511.05914 incident reporting design.

# What Counts as an 'AI Incident'? Measuring Definitional Drift Across Reporting Schemes

**Problem:** Different incident frameworks (OECD, EU AI Act, AIID, national regimes) define 'incident' differently, so the same event may be reportable in one jurisdiction and invisible in another — a hidden barrier to international coordination.

**Direction:** Collect the textual incident definitions and reporting triggers from 4-6 frameworks. Construct a set of ~30 real or synthetic borderline scenarios and use an LLM (prompted with each framework's definition) to judge reportability under each regime. Quantify divergence (which scenarios are reportable under N of K regimes) and map the definitional fault lines.

**Why it matters:** A common reporting framework cannot work if 'incident' means different things; surfacing the divergence empirically is a concrete, low-cost contribution to the national-incident-response and international-consensus open problems.

**Relevant context:** OECD 'Towards a common reporting framework for AI incidents' (29 criteria); AIID taxonomy; EU AI Act serious-incident reporting; The Future Society NTSB-analogy proposal.

# Probing an LLM as a 'Regulatory Compliance Judge': Reliability Under Prompt Variation

**Problem:** Governments and labs are starting to use LLMs to triage whether documents/practices comply with frameworks like the EU AI Act, but no one has measured how reliable an off-the-shelf LLM compliance judgment is when the same evidence is phrased differently.

**Direction:** Pick a concrete obligation (e.g. EU GPAI transparency documentation requirements). Create paired compliance scenarios that are semantically identical but vary in wording, ordering, and framing. Run an open model as a compliance judge and measure consistency, sensitivity to irrelevant cues, and susceptibility to 'compliance-washing' language. Report where automated compliance checking is and is not trustworthy.

**Why it matters:** If automated compliance judging is brittle, regulators relying on it will be gamed; this is a model-organism-style probe of a governance tool, doable on a single GPU with no proprietary data, and highly counterfactual.

**Relevant context:** EU GPAI Code of Practice (transparency, external evaluations); 'From Principles to Rules' arXiv:2407.07300; INESIA finding that small eval-design changes significantly affect results.

# Can LLM Evaluators Be Gamed by Compliance-Washing? An Adversarial Governance Probe

**Problem:** As safety frameworks push 'external evaluations' and automated documentation review, a medium-horizon risk is that providers learn to write documents that score well on automated checks without substantive safety — but no one has stress-tested automated governance judges against deliberate gaming.

**Direction:** Take a transparency/compliance rubric and a set of real model-card excerpts. Use simple rewriting strategies (keyword stuffing, hedged claims, confident but content-free language) to produce 'compliance-washed' variants and measure how much they inflate an open LLM judge's score versus human raters. Quantify the gaming gap and propose robustness checks.

**Why it matters:** Demonstrating that governance automation is gameable is exactly the kind of long-horizon, diffuse-reward red-teaming labs are forced to deprioritize; it needs no training and no proprietary access, and informs how regulators should design audits.

**Relevant context:** AI Transparency Atlas rubric; EU GPAI external-evaluation requirement; GovAI 'Frontier AI Auditing' note that models can intentionally underperform/mislead during evaluation.

**Direction:** On a tiny model (a small MLP or logistic-regression classifier), implement a minimal commitment/hash-based scheme that lets a 'verifier' confirm the deployed model's parameters match a previously committed snapshot, and show how a swapped model is detected. Discuss honestly what this toy demonstrates and what real ZK-ML/attestable audits add. Deliver runnable code plus an explainer blog post.

**Why it matters:** Bringing verifiable-audit primitives down to an understandable prototype builds the conceptual infrastructure governance needs (third-party verification of safety claims) and is fully doable on a consumer GPU with no proprietary models.

**Relevant context:** 'Attestable Audits' arXiv:2506.23706 (TEEs); ZK proofs for model-property verification; 'Frontier AI Auditing' GovAI AAL framework.

# A Minimal 'Compute Threshold Attestation' Demo for Training-Run Disclosure

**Problem:** Compute-governance proposals rely on developers credibly reporting when a training run exceeds a FLOP threshold, but the idea is abstract to newcomers and there is no small, inspectable demonstration of what 'attesting a training run's compute' could mean.

**Direction:** Build a toy training loop on a small model that logs a tamper-evident, hash-chained record of per-step FLOP estimates and total compute, producing a signed 'training-run certificate' a third party can check against a threshold without seeing the data. Discuss the trust assumptions, what a malicious developer could still fake, and where hardware-enabled mechanisms would be required.

**Why it matters:** Concretely prototyping compute attestation clarifies the 'balance safety with innovation' compute-governance open problem and the verification gap in export controls; it needs no real datacenter and is reproducible by anyone.

# Does More Disclosure Track Fewer Reported Incidents? A Correlational Probe

**Problem:** Governance assumes transparency improves safety, but the relationship between how much a provider discloses (transparency scores) and how many incidents its systems generate (incident databases) has never been examined empirically, even correlationally.

**Direction:** Join public transparency scores (FLI Index domains or a self-computed model-card score) with provider-attributed entries in the AIID/OECD AIM incident data. Run simple correlational and confounder-aware analysis (controlling for deployment scale/popularity as feasible) to ask whether disclosure correlates with incident counts/severity. Be explicit about causal limits and reporting bias.

**Why it matters:** Testing the core assumption of transparency-based governance — even imperfectly — is high-value and exactly the diffuse, fuzzy-reward analysis that needs no lab data; null or surprising results are informative either way.

**Relevant context:** FLI AI Safety Index domains; AIID / OECD AIM incident data; AI Transparency Atlas scoring.

**Direction:** Take a small open multilingual model and a fixed set of safety-relevant prompts (refusal, harmful-request handling). **Why it matters:** If safety evaluations are language-dependent, international consensus on methodology (an open problem) is undermined; this is a reproducible, single-GPU probe of an existing model that directly extends a Network finding without any lab resources.

**Problem:** Dynamic-safety-case research proposes structured arguments linking evidence to safety claims, but published safety frameworks rarely present explicit argument structure, so it is unknown whether their reasoning is even internally connected or just a list of activities.

**Direction:** Take published safety frameworks/cards and attempt to reconstruct each into a simple claim-argument-evidence graph (top claim 'this model is safe to deploy' -> sub-claims -> evidence). **Why it matters:** If safety cases are logically incomplete, the governance edifice resting on them is fragile; auditing argument structure from public text is a novel, low-cost contribution to verifiable safety claims.

**Why it matters:** If policy advice flows from a narrow, self-citing cluster, regulators may inherit shared blind spots; mapping this is a novel meta-governance analysis doable with basic Python/network tools and only public documents.

original_idea.body:
# Extending the FLI AI Safety Index to a 'broken-promise' tracking dimension

**Problem:** The FLI AI Safety Index (Summer/Winter 2025) scores 7 labs on 33 indicators across 6 domains using publicly verifiable evidence, but it scores the current state, not whether labs kept past public safety commitments. Commitment-drift is invisible in the snapshot.

**Direction:** Vary the Index methodology by adding a new dimension: track a curated set of dated public safety commitments (RSP pause clauses, eval promises, deployment gates) from lab blog posts/frameworks across two time points, and code whether each was kept, weakened, quietly dropped, or fulfilled. Produce a simple 'commitment integrity' sub-score per lab using a fixed rubric (0=reversed, 1=weakened, 2=unchanged, 3=strengthened).

**Why it matters:** Voluntary frameworks only constrain behavior if commitments persist; a reproducible drift tracker gives auditors and policymakers leverage the static Index lacks. It needs only public text, no lab access, and addresses the EU-AI-Office gap between voluntary codes and enforceable standards.

**Relevant context:** FLI AI Safety Index Summer/Winter 2025 (33 indicators, 6 domains, publicly verifiable evidence). Open Problems in Technical AI Governance (Reuel et al. 2024, arXiv:2407.14981) on third-party verification.

title: Re-running the 'Grading Rubric for AI Safety Frameworks' as an LLM-judge inter-rater study
quick_reasoning: Reliability check on automated safety-framework grading; well-targeted governance probe.

original_idea.body:
# Re-running the 'Grading Rubric for AI Safety Frameworks' as an LLM-judge inter-rater study

**Problem:** Alaga et al.'s grading rubric for AI safety frameworks (arXiv:2409.08751) was applied by human experts. We don't know how reliably an LLM judge reproduces those expert grades, or where it systematically diverges, which matters because automated grading is being proposed for scalable governance audits.

**Direction:** Take the published rubric and the publicly available frontier safety frameworks (Anthropic RSP, DeepMind FSF, OpenAI Preparedness, Meta), have an off-the-shelf LLM grade each framework against each rubric criterion with chain-of-thought, then compute agreement (Cohen's kappa) against any published human grades and across 3 prompt variants / 2 models for self-consistency.

**Why it matters:** If LLM judges are inconsistent or biased on governance text, automated framework-grading proposals are premature. This is a cheap, counterfactually valuable reliability check requiring only public docs and API calls, no training.

**Relevant context:** A Grading Rubric for AI Safety Frameworks (Alaga et al., arXiv:2409.08751); METR 'Common Elements of Frontier AI Safety Policies'; LLM-as-judge calibration via Cohen's kappa / Krippendorff's alpha.

title: Varying the METR 'Common Elements' analysis across model versions of the same lab
quick_reasoning: Surfaces safety-commitment erosion within a lab over time; clear governance relevance.

original_idea.body:
# Varying the METR 'Common Elements' analysis across model versions of the same lab

**Problem:** METR's 'Common Elements of Frontier AI Safety Policies' compares elements across labs at one time. It does not study how a single lab's framework evolves across successive versions (e.g., Anthropic RSP v1 -> v2.x), where commitments may silently soften.

**Direction:** Vary METR's cross-lab comparison into a within-lab longitudinal comparison. Collect every public version of one or two labs' frameworks, diff them section-by-section against METR's element checklist, and code each change as added/removed/loosened/tightened with quotes. Visualize commitment trajectories per element.

**Why it matters:** Surfaces a governance failure mode (commitment erosion under competitive pressure) invisible to snapshot comparisons, using only archived public documents. Directly informs whether voluntary frameworks ratchet up or down over time.

**Relevant context:** METR 'Common Elements of Frontier AI Safety Policies' (2024); Anthropic Responsible Scaling Policy versions; FAS 'Can Preparedness Frameworks Pull Their Weight?' (underspecification critique).

title: Specificity/hedging linguistic audit of frontier safety frameworks
quick_reasoning: Quantifies vagueness of safety commitments, a recognized governance measurement gap.

original_idea.body:
# Specificity/hedging linguistic audit of frontier safety frameworks

**Problem:** Critiques (FAS, METR) say frontier safety frameworks are 'underspecified', but specificity is asserted qualitatively, not measured. There is no reproducible metric for how vague a commitment is.

**Direction:** Vary qualitative framework critique into a quantitative text experiment: build a small lexicon-based + LLM-classifier pipeline that tags each commitment sentence in public frameworks as binding ('will', 'must', dated) vs. hedged ('aim to', 'where feasible', 'consider'), and computes a hedging ratio per lab and per risk domain (CBRN, cyber, autonomy). Compare labs and correlate hedging with FLI Index scores.

**Why it matters:** Gives policymakers a cheap, reproducible vagueness metric to push for enforceable language, addressing the explicit EU-AI-Office gap between voluntary codes and enforceable standards. No lab access, public text only.

**Relevant context:** FAS 'Can Preparedness Frameworks Pull Their Weight?'; METR Common Elements; EU AI Act GPAI Code of Practice; Measurement challenges in AI catastrophic risk governance (arXiv:2410.00608).

title: Replicating the AI Transparency Atlas scoring on a held-out set of model/system cards
quick_reasoning: Independent replication of a safety-transparency governance metric; well-targeted.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating the AI Transparency Atlas scoring on a held-out set of model/system cards

**Problem:** The AI Transparency Atlas (arXiv:2512.12443) built a weighted 8-section transparency framework and scored ~50 models, finding frontier labs at ~80% and most providers below 60%. The pipeline's robustness on new, unseen cards and to scoring-prompt variation is untested by independent parties.

**Direction:** Vary the experiment to a replication-on-new-data study: apply the published weighted rubric (Safety Eval 25%, Critical Risk 20%, etc.) to a fresh sample of 15-20 recent Hugging Face / lab model cards not in the original set, score them with an LLM judge, and report whether the 80%-vs-60% frontier gap holds and how sensitive scores are to rubric-prompt phrasing.

**Why it matters:** Independent replication is the backbone of credible third-party transparency audits. Confirms or challenges a published governance metric using only public model cards and no training.

**Relevant context:** AI Transparency Atlas (arXiv:2512.12443); Stanford Foundation Model Transparency Index; EU AI Act Annex IV documentation requirements.

title: AI Incident Database taxonomy stress-test: does an LLM reproduce CSET harm classifications?
quick_reasoning: Tests reliability of incident classification underpinning governance trend analyses.

original_idea.body:
# AI Incident Database taxonomy stress-test: does an LLM reproduce CSET harm classifications?

**Problem:** The AIID re-classifies incident reports via LLM tools against the CSET and MIT AI Risk taxonomies, but the reliability of LLM classification against human-coded ground truth on these specific taxonomies is underexamined, and misclassification distorts trend analyses used by policymakers.

**Direction:** Vary the AIID's automated classification setup into an evaluation experiment: sample incidents that already have human CSET-taxonomy labels, have an LLM re-classify them blind under the same taxonomy, compute per-category agreement (kappa) and a confusion matrix, and identify which harm categories the model systematically conflates.

**Why it matters:** An NTSB-style AI incident response framework (a listed open problem) depends on trustworthy incident classification. This exposes where automated coding biases the evidence base, using a fully public dataset.

**Relevant context:** AI Incident Database (incidentdatabase.ai); CSET AI Harm Taxonomy; 'Automating AI Failure Tracking' (arXiv:2507.23669); MIT AI Risk Taxonomy.

title: Trend re-analysis of the AI Incident Database: are agentic/autonomy incidents rising?
quick_reasoning: Quantifies rising agentic-AI incident risk to inform incident-response governance.

original_idea.body:
# Trend re-analysis of the AI Incident Database: are agentic/autonomy incidents rising?

**Problem:** The AIID has 1,300+ incidents but most trend analyses predate the agentic-AI wave. Whether the composition of incidents is shifting toward autonomy/agent failures (a frontier safety concern) is not quantified.

**Direction:** Vary prior AIID trend studies along the time and category axes: bucket incidents by year and re-tag a sample for an 'agentic/autonomy' flag using a keyword+LLM classifier, then plot the share of agentic incidents over time and test for a significant upward trend (chi-square / simple regression).

**Why it matters:** Empirically grounds the policy claim that agentic AI introduces new risk classes, informing incident-response framework design. Pure public-data analysis, no lab resources, medium-horizon threat focus.

**Relevant context:** AI Incident Database; 'Incident Analysis for AI Agents' (arXiv:2508.14231); MIT AI Incident Tracker (5,499 reports / 1,366 incidents as of 2026).

title: Replicating Epoch compute-trend extrapolations and stress-testing threshold model counts
quick_reasoning: Tests robustness of compute-governance thresholds, a core governance lever.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating Epoch compute-trend extrapolations and stress-testing threshold model counts

**Problem:** Epoch projects ~30 models above 1e26 FLOP by 2027 and 4-5x/year compute growth, numbers that directly underpin compute-governance thresholds (e.g., EU AI Act 1e25 FLOP, US 1e26). The sensitivity of these counts to fit choices and threshold placement is rarely re-derived independently.

**Direction:** Vary Epoch's analysis by re-fitting the growth curve on the public Notable Models dataset, then sweep the regulatory threshold (1e24..1e27) and recompute how many models cross each by year. Report how regulated-model counts swing with threshold choice and with including/excluding open models.

**Why it matters:** Compute thresholds are a core governance lever; showing how brittle 'models-above-threshold' counts are to assumptions helps regulators set defensible cutoffs. Uses Epoch's public CSV, beginner-friendly regression, no training.

**Relevant context:** Epoch AI Notable Models dataset (450+ entries); 'Training compute grows 4-5x/year'; 'How many AI models will exceed compute thresholds?'; Trends in Frontier AI Model Count (arXiv:2504.16138).

title: Security vs. innovation framing: does an institute's name predict its publication mix?
quick_reasoning: Tests whether institute framing shapes safety output; clear governance relevance.

original_idea.body:
# Security vs. innovation framing: does an institute's name predict its publication mix?

**Problem:** UK AISI rebranded to 'AI Security Institute' (security framing) while US AISI became CAISI (innovation framing). The surprising-result note asks whether these divergent framings correlate with different safety outputs, but no measurement exists.

**Direction:** Vary the qualitative observation into a content-analysis experiment: scrape public outputs (reports, blog posts, blueprints) from a set of national AI safety/security institutes, code each output's primary emphasis (security/misuse vs. innovation/adoption vs. catastrophic-risk) with a fixed rubric + LLM classifier, and test whether framing branding predicts output emphasis.

**Why it matters:** Tests whether institutional framing is cosmetic or shapes what gets worked on, informing how the International Network of AISIs should coordinate. Fully public text, no lab access.

**Relevant context:** Subfield surprising result: UK AISI -> AI Security Institute, US AISI -> CAISI; International Network of AI Safety Institutes.

title: Cross-jurisdiction commitment-gap analysis: EU GPAI Code of Practice vs. lab self-frameworks
quick_reasoning: Maps safety-commitment gaps between EU Code and labs; well-targeted governance work.

original_idea.body:
# Cross-jurisdiction commitment-gap analysis: EU GPAI Code of Practice vs. lab self-frameworks

**Problem:** EU GPAI Code of Practice (final version, enforcement from Aug 2026) and individual lab frameworks both make safety-and-security commitments, but where they diverge or where labs commit to less than the Code is not systematically mapped.

**Direction:** Vary single-document framework analyses into a gap-matrix experiment: extract atomic commitments from the EU Code's Safety & Security chapter and from each signatory lab's own framework, align them, and code each pair as Code-stronger / equal / lab-stronger / no-coverage. Produce a coverage heatmap per lab.

**Why it matters:** Directly maps the EU-AI-Office's flagged gap between voluntary codes and lab practice on the eve of enforcement, giving regulators a concrete list of under-covered commitments. Public text only.

**Relevant context:** EU AI Act GPAI Code of Practice (code-of-practice.ai, Safety & Security chapter, enforcement 2 Aug 2026); lab frameworks (Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepMind).

title: Robustness of frontier-safety-framework grading to adversarial document rephrasing
quick_reasoning: Quantifies gaming vulnerability of automated safety-framework grading; well-targeted.

original_idea.body:
# Robustness of frontier-safety-framework grading to adversarial document rephrasing

**Problem:** If governance audits use LLM judges to grade safety frameworks, a lab could 'game' the grade by rephrasing vague commitments to sound concrete. Whether current LLM graders are fooled by such cosmetic rewrites is unknown.

**Direction:** Vary the grading experiment with an adversarial-perturbation arm: take real framework excerpts, create matched rewrites that add confident-sounding but non-binding language (no actual stronger commitment), and measure how much an LLM judge's grade inflates. Report the 'rhetoric premium' per rubric criterion.

**Why it matters:** Quantifies a concrete gaming vulnerability in automated governance audits before they are deployed, a medium-horizon institutional risk. Cheap, public-text, no training, high counterfactual value for non-lab auditors.

**Relevant context:** A Grading Rubric for AI Safety Frameworks (arXiv:2409.08751); LLM-as-judge biases; Open Problems in Technical AI Governance (third-party auditing with black-box access).

title: Replicating CBRN-as-top-risk consensus and checking threshold comparability across labs
quick_reasoning: Tests comparability of CBRN safety thresholds across labs; clear governance relevance.

original_idea.body:
# Replicating CBRN-as-top-risk consensus and checking threshold comparability across labs

**Problem:** A review found near-universal industry consensus that CBRN is the highest risk tier, but each lab defines its capability thresholds differently (ASL-4, Critical Risk, Catastrophic Malicious Use), making 'consensus' possibly superficial and thresholds non-comparable.

**Direction:** Vary the consensus-review experiment by operationalizing comparability: extract each lab's CBRN threshold definition and triggered mitigations, then have annotators + an LLM map them onto a common scale (capability described, eval specified, mitigation specified, pause committed). Score how comparable the 'same' top tier really is.

**Why it matters:** International evaluation consensus (a listed open problem) is hollow if top-tier thresholds aren't comparable. This produces a concrete comparability scorecard from public frameworks, no lab access.

**Relevant context:** 'Quantifying CBRN Risk in Frontier Models' (arXiv:2510.21133); Frontier Safety Frameworks comparative review; Evaluating AI Companies' Frontier Safety Frameworks (arXiv:2512.01166).

title: Reproducing the FLI Index 'existential safety' scoring with an independent rubric pass
quick_reasoning: Independent reproduction of existential-safety scoring; directly safety-governance relevant.

original_idea.body:
# Reproducing the FLI Index 'existential safety' scoring with an independent rubric pass

**Problem:** FLI's most damning finding is that no lab has an adequate existential-safety plan, scored by a small expert panel. Independent reproducibility of this specific, contestable judgment using only public evidence has not been tested.

**Direction:** Vary the Index by isolating the existential-safety domain and re-scoring it independently: define a transparent sub-rubric (does a plan exist? is it dated? does it name a control/alignment approach? does it commit to a stop condition?), apply it to public lab statements, and compare the resulting ranking to FLI's. Document where independent scoring agrees/diverges.

**Why it matters:** Tests whether the headline 'no adequate existential plan' result is robust to who scores it, strengthening (or qualifying) a widely-cited governance claim. Public statements only, beginner-feasible rubric coding.

**Relevant context:** FLI AI Safety Index Summer/Winter 2025 (existential safety domain, no lab above C+); MIRI 'AI Governance to Avoid Extinction' (2025).

title: Bug-bounty / responsible-disclosure policy comparison across AI vendors
quick_reasoning: Compares vendor policies on reporting model harms, relevant to safety-research governance.

original_idea.body:
# Bug-bounty / responsible-disclosure policy comparison across AI vendors

**Problem:** Research notes 'abuse risks are often inherent to product features' and examines AI vendors' bug-bounty and responsible-disclosure policies, but a structured, comparable scorecard of what AI labs actually allow safety researchers to report (model harms vs. only classic security bugs) is thin.

**Direction:** Vary the disclosure-policy study into a structured comparison experiment: collect public bug-bounty/disclosure terms from major AI vendors, code each on a fixed checklist (covers model-behavior harms? safe-harbor for jailbreak research? response SLA? scope exclusions?), and produce a vendor comparison table plus a 'researcher-friendliness' score.

**Why it matters:** External red-teaming and incident reporting are key governance mechanisms; showing where policies discourage safety research is actionable for the NTSB-style incident-framework open problem. Public terms only.

**Relevant context:** 'Abuse Risks are Often Inherent to Product Features' (arXiv:2509.06136); Open Problems in Technical AI Governance (third-party auditing); The Future Society NTSB-analogy proposal.

title: Varying the transparency-index unit of analysis from labs to open-weight model releases
quick_reasoning: Audits open-weight safety disclosure gaps; well-targeted governance work.

original_idea.body:
# Varying the transparency-index unit of analysis from labs to open-weight model releases

**Problem:** Transparency indices (Stanford FMTI, AI Transparency Atlas) focus heavily on major closed/frontier labs. Open-weight releases on Hugging Face, which proliferate fastest, are under-audited for safety-critical disclosure despite being the most easily redistributed.

**Direction:** Vary the population studied: apply a compact transparency rubric (data provenance, safety eval, intended-use/misuse limits, license) to a stratified sample of the most-downloaded open-weight models on Hugging Face, and compare disclosure completeness against frontier labs. Quantify the open-weight transparency gap.

**Why it matters:** Open-weight proliferation is a medium-horizon governance frontier that big labs deprioritize; documenting their disclosure gaps is high counterfactual value and uses only public model cards.

**Relevant context:** AI Transparency Atlas (arXiv:2512.12443, 100 HF cards, 947 section names); Stanford FMTI; Epoch note that frontier open models may surpass 1e26 FLOP.

title: Are 'capability threshold' definitions measurable? An operationalizability audit
quick_reasoning: Scores operationalizability of capability thresholds triggering safety measures.

original_idea.body:
# Are 'capability threshold' definitions measurable? An operationalizability audit

**Problem:** RSP-style frameworks define capability thresholds that trigger safety measures, but Open Problems in Technical AI Governance flags the gap between safety objectives and operationalizable deployment practice. Many thresholds may be unmeasurable as written.

**Direction:** Vary framework analysis into an operationalizability coding experiment: extract every capability threshold from public frameworks and code each on whether it names (a) a concrete benchmark/eval, (b) a numeric or behavioral trigger, (c) who decides, (d) a deadline. Compute an 'operationalizability score' per threshold and per lab.

**Why it matters:** Translates the abstract operationalization open problem into a measurable scorecard regulators can use to demand testable triggers. Public text, beginner rubric coding, no lab access.

**Relevant context:** Open Problems in Technical AI Governance (Reuel et al., arXiv:2407.14981, operationalization); METR Common Elements; Measurement challenges in AI catastrophic risk governance (arXiv:2410.00608).

title: Testing whether LLM policy-summaries preserve binding commitments (faithfulness audit)
quick_reasoning: Tests whether automated summarization distorts safety commitments; clear governance relevance.

original_idea.body:
# Testing whether LLM policy-summaries preserve binding commitments (faithfulness audit)

**Problem:** Policymakers and journalists increasingly rely on LLM summaries of long safety frameworks. If summarization systematically drops hedges or upgrades 'aims' to 'commits', it distorts the governance record, but this faithfulness has not been measured on safety policy text.

**Direction:** Vary commitment-extraction into a summary-faithfulness experiment: have an LLM summarize public framework sections, then check each summary sentence against the source for commitment-strength fidelity (added commitments, dropped caveats, strength inflation) using a human-built gold set, and report error rates by error type.

**Why it matters:** AI is increasingly in the loop of governing AI; showing where automated summarization misrepresents commitments is a concrete, infrastructure-relevant safety finding. Public text + API only.

**Relevant context:** EU GPAI Code of Practice; lab frameworks; LLM-as-judge / faithfulness evaluation literature; Open Problems in Technical AI Governance.

title: Cross-national divergence in dangerous-capability eval requirements
quick_reasoning: Maps divergence in safety-eval requirements across jurisdictions; well-targeted.

original_idea.body:
# Cross-national divergence in dangerous-capability eval requirements

**Problem:** Establishing international consensus on AI evaluation methodologies is a listed open problem, but the actual divergence between jurisdictions' eval expectations (EU Code, UK AISI guidance, US/CAISI, voluntary commitments) has not been mapped side by side.

**Direction:** Vary single-jurisdiction policy reads into a comparative requirements matrix: extract evaluation-related requirements from each jurisdiction's public document, code each on dimensions (which risk domains, who runs the eval, pre- vs post-deployment, disclosure required), and quantify overlap/divergence with a similarity score.

**Why it matters:** Concretely measures how far apart the international eval landscape is, informing the International Network of AISIs' harmonization efforts. Public policy text, beginner-feasible coding.

**Relevant context:** International Network of AI Safety Institutes; EU GPAI Code of Practice; UK AI Security Institute; International Scientific Report on the Safety of Advanced AI (arXiv:2412.05282).

title: Does the FLI Index correlate with the Stanford Transparency Index? A cross-instrument validity check
quick_reasoning: Meta-validity check of governance scorecards; safety relevance present but indirect.

original_idea.body:
# Does the FLI Index correlate with the Stanford Transparency Index? A cross-instrument validity check

**Problem:** Multiple governance scorecards (FLI Safety Index, Stanford FMTI, AI Transparency Atlas) rank overlapping labs, but whether they agree, i.e. measure a shared underlying 'safety/transparency' construct, is untested. Disagreement would undermine all of them.

**Direction:** Vary single-index analysis into a convergent-validity experiment: assemble per-lab scores from 2-3 public indices for the overlapping set of labs, compute rank correlations (Spearman) and per-domain agreement, and identify labs where indices sharply disagree and why.

**Why it matters:** If governance indices don't converge, policymakers can cherry-pick; quantifying their (dis)agreement is essential meta-evaluation. Uses only published scores, trivial compute, beginner statistics.

**Relevant context:** FLI AI Safety Index Summer/Winter 2025; Stanford Foundation Model Transparency Index; AI Transparency Atlas (arXiv:2512.12443).

title: Reproducibility of an LLM-based AI-policy compliance checker across model families
quick_reasoning: Tests cross-model stability of automated governance auditing; well-targeted.

original_idea.body:
# Reproducibility of an LLM-based AI-policy compliance checker across model families

**Problem:** LLM-as-judge is proposed for scalable policy-adherence checking, but governance-critical decisions need cross-model stability. If GPT-class, Claude-class, and open models grade the same policy document differently, automated compliance checks are unreliable.

**Direction:** Vary the judge model: run the same compliance rubric over the same set of safety frameworks with 3+ different LLM families (incl. an open-weight model runnable on a single GPU), then measure inter-model agreement and systematic per-model leniency/strictness biases.

**Why it matters:** Establishes whether automated governance auditing is robust to model choice, a prerequisite before any institution adopts it. Counterfactually valuable, runnable on consumer hardware with an open model, no training.

**Relevant context:** LLM-as-judge calibration (kappa, agreement metrics); A Grading Rubric for AI Safety Frameworks (arXiv:2409.08751); METR Common Elements.

title: Time-to-disclosure analysis: how fast do labs publish safety evals after model release?
quick_reasoning: Quantifies safety-disclosure lag undermining pre-deployment governance; well-targeted.

original_idea.body:
# Time-to-disclosure analysis: how fast do labs publish safety evals after model release?

**Problem:** System/model cards are central to deployment governance, but whether safety-relevant disclosures arrive before, with, or after release, and how that lag has changed, is not quantified. Late disclosure undermines pre-deployment governance.

**Direction:** Vary static transparency scoring into a temporal experiment: for a set of frontier model releases, record release date vs. system-card / safety-eval publication date (from archives/Wayback), compute disclosure lag, and test for a trend over time and across labs.

**Why it matters:** Pre-deployment evaluation is meaningless if disclosure trails release; a reproducible lag metric pressures labs and informs EU AI Act timing requirements. Public timestamps only, no lab access.

**Relevant context:** AI Transparency Atlas (arXiv:2512.12443); EU AI Act Annex IV; Open Problems in Technical AI Governance (pre-deployment assessment).

title: Sensitivity of compute-governance exemptions: who falls through open-weight / fine-tuning loopholes?
quick_reasoning: Quantifies high-capability models escaping compute-governance oversight; clear safety relevance.

original_idea.body:
# Sensitivity of compute-governance exemptions: who falls through open-weight / fine-tuning loopholes?

**Problem:** Many compute-governance rules exempt open-source models or apply only to base-model training FLOP, not fine-tuning. Whether these carve-outs let high-capability systems escape oversight is asserted but not quantified against real model data.

**Direction:** Vary the threshold-counting experiment to model exemptions: using Epoch's Notable Models data plus public fine-tune/open-weight flags, simulate which models are captured vs. exempted under different rule variants (base-only vs. cumulative compute, open-weight exemption on/off) and report the exempted high-compute population.

**Why it matters:** Shows concretely how much capability slips through compute-governance loopholes, a medium-horizon proliferation risk labs deprioritize. Public dataset, beginner data analysis, no training.

**Relevant context:** Epoch AI Notable Models dataset; 'How many AI models will exceed compute thresholds?'; EU AI Act 1e25 FLOP / US 1e26 FLOP thresholds; MIRI compute-governance agenda.

title: Are AI incident reports actionable? Coding root-cause and mitigation completeness
quick_reasoning: Measures actionability of incident reports for NTSB-style AI safety governance.

original_idea.body:
# Are AI incident reports actionable? Coding root-cause and mitigation completeness

**Problem:** An NTSB-style AI incident framework requires reports rich enough to drive mitigations, but most AIID entries are media reports. How often incidents include identifiable root causes and mitigations, the inputs an NTSB process needs, is unmeasured.

**Direction:** Vary AIID analysis toward actionability: sample incidents and code each for presence of (a) identifiable proximate cause, (b) system/lifecycle stage, (c) any documented mitigation, (d) accountable party, using a fixed rubric + LLM assist. Report what fraction of the record is NTSB-actionable.

**Why it matters:** Quantifies the evidentiary gap an AI-incident-response institution would face, directly informing the NTSB-analogy open problem. Fully public data, beginner coding task.

**Relevant context:** AI Incident Database; 'Lessons for Editors of AI Incidents' (arXiv:2409.16425); The Future Society NTSB-for-AI proposal; CSET AI Harm Taxonomy.

title: Prompt-sensitivity of dangerous-capability eval scores as a governance reliability concern
quick_reasoning: Targets a specific AI Safety problem (brittleness of dangerous-capability eval scores used to trigger governance) with a focused empirical approach.

original_idea.body:
# Prompt-sensitivity of dangerous-capability eval scores as a governance reliability concern

**Problem:** Governance increasingly relies on dangerous-capability eval scores to trigger safety measures, yet such scores can swing with prompt phrasing. If a 'below-threshold' result flips 'above-threshold' under benign prompt variation, threshold-based governance is fragile.

**Direction:** Vary the eval-administration conditions on a public safety-relevant benchmark (e.g., a hazardous-knowledge proxy like a WMDP-style public subset) using a small open model on a single GPU: run the same items under several harmless prompt/format variations and quantify score variance and how often it crosses a hypothetical threshold.

**Why it matters:** Demonstrates that threshold-triggered governance commitments inherit eval brittleness, a measurement-validity problem regulators must account for. Counterfactual value: needs only a public benchmark and one consumer GPU.

**Relevant context:** Measurement challenges in AI catastrophic risk governance (arXiv:2410.00608); RSP capability thresholds; public hazardous-capability benchmarks (WMDP); Open Problems in Technical AI Governance (assessment).
